Coach's note, under-11 football, Saturday. Francis sir.
Before today's final, I asked each boy to write his predicted score on the whiteboard. Samir wrote "We win 3–1" in big letters and drew a trophy. We lost 0–2. In the van home, Samir told the others, "I knew we'd lose. Their goalkeeper was too tall. It was obvious from the start." When Farhan pointed out his whiteboard prediction, Samir said he had "secretly known." He seemed to truly believe it.
What I did: I took a photo of the whiteboard. Next week I'll show it at practice, not to shame anyone, but to talk about how our memory changes after a match.

Sunday
Our colony team lost the gully cricket final to C-block today. I knew it all along. Their bowler was too fast and our captain kept dropping catches. Anyone could see it. Alka said, "But yesterday you bet me five toffees we'd win by fifty runs!" That was different. I was just being nice to the team. Jasleen said I made a poster that said CHAMPIONS. That was for fun. Deep inside I always knew. Mummy laughed and called me her know-it-all boy. I don't think it's funny. I'm going to write my prediction for next week here, so nobody can argue.
Jatin

"Well… I sort of knew." Noa laughed. "You knew after it happened." Hiroshi frowned, trying to remember what he really thought that morning. Now the loss seemed certain too. He handed her the dessert anyway.

"I heard 'no chance for the other one.'" A few boys laughed. Chaitanya went pink. "It felt like I knew," he said quietly. Lalit sir nodded. "It always does, afterwards."

passage: Wasim, you said you knew your team would lose yesterday. Let your Amandeep uncle tell you about the hockey final at our village mela when I was nine. Before the match, I told everyone our side would win for sure. I even climbed a tree to watch. We lost, four goals to one. Walking home, I told my father, "I knew it. Their centre-forward was too fast. I could see it from the start." My father stopped walking. "Amandeep, this morning you told the whole lane we'd win." I was angry, because in my head I really had known. It felt like a memory, not a story I had just made. My father wasn't cross. He said, "Next time, tell me your guess, and I'll remember it for you." So before every match I told him, and he always remembered.

I'm Amandeep. Last Lohri, we watched the big kabaddi match in the village with everyone, next to the bonfire.

Before it started, I said to my sister Vidya, "Punjab will win easily." Then Haryana scored first and I said, "Okay, maybe Haryana." Then Punjab came back and I shouted, "PUNJAB!"

Haryana won in the end.

After the match, I told my cousins, "I knew Haryana would win. It was obvious." And I really felt like I had known.

Vidya laughed so hard she nearly dropped her rewri. "You said Punjab! Three times!"

I said I only said it to cheer. But then I remembered. I really had thought Punjab would win.

My mind had changed the story afterwards to make me look clever.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Sports Day, December

Pradeep's house, Blue, lost the relay today. Before the race, I heard Pradeep say to Nirmala, "Blue will definitely win, we've got the fastest runners." Halfway through, when Blue dropped the baton, he said, "Maybe Green now."

After the race, which Yellow won, Pradeep told his group, "I knew Yellow would win. Everyone could see it." When Nirmala reminded him of what he'd said earlier, he became upset and insisted he had always known.

I think he really believed it. Children often tidy up memories after the fact.

In class later, we did a small activity: everyone wrote down a guess for tomorrow's football match before it happened, in sealed envelopes. Pradeep liked the idea.

We'll open the envelopes on Friday.

qa.q: Which house won the relay?
qa.a: Yellow won.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep become upset when Nirmala reminded him?
qa.a: Pradeep felt embarrassed and defensive, because he truly believed he had always known, and being reminded challenged that.

qa.q: Why was the sealed envelope activity a good idea?
qa.a: It records guesses before the result, so later memories can't be quietly rewritten.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when Pradeep insisted he had always known?
qa.a: Nirmala may have felt frustrated or confused, since Nirmala clearly remembered what Pradeep had said.

Dear Diary,
Ganpati festival, day 5.

Tonight was the kabaddi final in our building compound, Wing A vs Wing C. Before it started, Tanuja asked me who'd win. I said Wing A for sure. I even bet her my modak.

Then Wing C won by two points.

At dinner, I told Aai and Baba, "I knew Wing C would win. Their raider was so strong." And it felt true when I said it.

But Tanuja was sitting right there. She said, "You bet me your modak on Wing A!"

I went red. She was right. I had totally forgotten. My brain made up a new story where I was smart.

I gave her the modak.

Tomorrow, I'll write my guess down BEFORE the match.

Madhav
